texts.facts: The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 23.6.1992 at about 12.15 p.m., PW1 the Food Inspector, Navaikulam Panchayat, purchased 375 grams of gingely oil from the shop of the first accused. First accused was the salesman. Fifth accused was the firm and accused Nos.2 to 5 were the partners of the firm. After sampling, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst. The Public Analyst filed Ext. P10 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for gingely oil under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1956 and therefore, the same was adulterated. On the request of the revision petitioner, another sample was sent for the examination to the Central Food Laboratory. Ext.P15 report of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for gingelly oil and therefore, it was adulterated. Thereafter, complaint was filed before the court by the Food Inspector after complying with the legal formalities. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW4 were examined and Exts. P1 to P34 were marked for the prosecution. DW1 was examined and Exts.D1 to D3 were marked for the revision petitioner. 6. In this case, Admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P15 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. 2 petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
